name: PuppyGraph
license: Proprietary; the Developer Edition is free
summary: A graph query engine that reads tables where they already live, in Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, warehouses and SQL databases, and answers openCypher and Gremlin queries without loading the data into a graph database.
intro: PuppyGraph stores no data of its own. You connect it to catalogs and databases, then describe a graph in one JSON schema: each node type points at a table and its key columns, and each edge type points at a table plus the key columns that match the nodes at either end. The schema can be written by hand, built in the web UI’s schema builder, or proposed by PuppyGraph AI after it inspects the tables, and it can be edited in place later. At query time PuppyGraph compiles a graph query into a plan of node and edge operators and runs it in its own distributed, auto-sharded engine, sending only simple projection and filter SQL to the source. Connectors cover Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi and Hive tables, catalogs such as Unity Catalog, Polaris, Nessie, Amazon S3 Tables and OneLake, and databases including PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift and Trino.

Clients reach it through a web UI and REST API on port 8081, a Gremlin server on 8182 and openCypher over the Bolt protocol on 7687. The Developer Edition is free forever but runs on a single node in Docker; the Enterprise Edition has a 30-day trial, runs in Docker, on an AWS AMI or from Helm charts and marketplace listings, and is priced by the memory and CPU of the machines it runs on. PuppyGraph’s own figures include a six-hop query over 600 million edges in under a second. It launched in March 2024 and released version 1.15.1 on 17 October 2026.
strengths: No second copy and no ETL pipeline: the graph reads the same governed tables as SQL and BI tools, so it is as fresh as those tables
The graph is only a mapping, so adding or reshaping node and edge types means editing the schema, not reloading data
Works over many sources at once, from Iceberg and Delta Lake tables to Postgres, Snowflake and BigQuery
Standard languages and protocols, openCypher over Bolt and Gremlin, so existing graph drivers and tools connect
limits: Closed source, and Enterprise pricing is not published
Columnar tables are laid out for scans, not for following a few edges at a time; PuppyGraph itself says low-latency point traversals and write-heavy graph workloads fit a graph database better
Edges are only as good as the keys in the tables: entity resolution and choosing which relationships to model are up to you, and very high-degree nodes can blow up a hop
Independent numbers are scarce: a 2026 paper by TigerGraph and Purdue researchers reported PuppyGraph running out of memory on some LDBC queries and graph algorithms where their own engine finished

story: PuppyGraph was founded by Weimo Liu, who had worked on Google’s F1 team and at TigerGraph, with Danfeng Xu, a long-time LinkedIn infrastructure engineer, and Lei Huang. In a February 2023 talk for the Trino community, Liu argued that many users want a graph data lake rather than a graph database: they don’t want to load data twice, keep two copies in sync, or pay for a graph server that can’t be turned off without losing its data.

The product launched in March 2024, and in November 2024 the company raised a $5 million seed round led by defy.vc, naming Coinbase and Clarivate among production users and describing itself as Databricks’ first graph analytics partner for Unity Catalog. By 2026 it had added catalog integrations from Polaris to OneLake, a Snowflake Native App and an AI assistant that proposes graph schemas, and it promotes the term “graph lakehouse” for graph queries over open table formats.

choices.choice: A query engine with no storage of its own
choices.why: Graph databases tie the query layer to their own storage, which forces a copy of the data and an ETL pipeline. Keeping data in the lake means the engine can be stopped after a query and the data stays put.

choices.choice: The graph defined as a mapping over tables
choices.why: Node and edge types point at existing tables and keys, so the same rows serve SQL and graph queries and the model can change without a reload.

choices.choice: Gremlin and openCypher rather than a new language
choices.why: Both already have drivers, tools and users, so teams can query the lake as a graph with what they know.
